Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- A fire that claimed the lives of 44 children at a day-care center in Hermosillo, Mexico, started Friday in an air-conditioning unit in an adjacent warehouse, the attorney general of Sonora said Monday. Maria Jesus Coronado Padilla mourns her daughter, Paulette Daniela Coronado Padilla, 2, on Sunday. Investigators have not determined whether the fire was caused by an overheated motor or deficiencies in its installation, said Abel Murrieta Gutierrez, according to the state-run news agency Notimex. However it started, there's no doubt it moved toward papers in bookshelves on the wall shared with the building housing ABC Day Care, where 141 children and day-care workers were, he said. The two buildings also shared a roof, which contained a false bottom made of polyurethane, which overheated, emitting highly toxic fumes, he said. He blamed all 44 of the deaths on the fumes. The general director of the Mexican Institute of Social Security vowed  investigators will pursue the case wherever the evidence takes them. Daniel Karam Toumeh had said Sunday that the building had passed an inspection on May 26. "Here, I want to be very emphatic, in the sense that in Social Security we don't cover for anyone, don't defend anyone, we are the most interested in finding out what it was that happened," he said. As of Monday morning, 20 children ages 1-5 were hospitalized in Hermosillo, and 13 had been taken to other hospitals, including three to Sacramento Shriners Hospital in California, where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty.  Watch parents gather at the site of the fire » . Hermosillo, the capital of the state of Sonora, is about 200 miles (320 kilometers) south of the U.S. border in northwestern Mexico. On a radio show, a firefighter said Monday that many of the children were napping at the time of the fire and died in their sleep. Jose Jesus Diaz, the first firefighter to enter the day-care center, told Radio Los Cheros that he arrived to find some people ramming the building with their vehicles in an effort to reach the children. Inside, Diaz said, he saw children in sleeping positions on the floor. "They never knew what happened," Diaz told the radio station. The scene was one of people crying, calling out names and running with babies, he said. "There's an image that I will carry for the rest of my life: a shirtless man walking outside holding a young boy, yelling 'fireman, fireman, save my son,' but the boy was already dead," Diaz said.  Watch a town in deep shock » . Of the 20 children hospitalized in Hermosillo, 12 were in serious condition. The children taken to Children's Hospital in Sacramento are a 2-year-old boy in serious condition with burns over 20 percent of his body, a 3-year-old boy in critical condition with burns over 50 percent of his body, and a 3-year-old girl in critical condition with burns over 80 percent of her body, a hospital spokeswoman said. CNN's Mariano Castillo in Atlanta and CNN en Español's Rey Rodriguez in Hermosillo contributed to this story.

# 2009 Hermosillo day-care fire: Investigators cited electrical failure, flammable materials and failed safeguards

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico** — Thick black smoke poured from a government warehouse and swept into an adjoining day-care center on June 5, 2009, trapping scores of infants and young children as employees, parents and bystanders fought to reach them.

The fire at the privately operated **ABC Day Care Center** in Hermosillo, capital of the northern Mexican state of Sonora, ultimately killed **49 children** and injured more than 100 others. Most of the victims were babies, toddlers and preschoolers.

It became one of Mexico’s deadliest child-care disasters and triggered years of investigations, criminal proceedings and protests by families who accused officials of allowing a poorly protected facility to operate.

## Fire began in adjoining warehouse

Investigators determined that the blaze originated in a warehouse next to the day-care center. The building was being used by the Sonora state government to store documents, vehicle license plates and other materials.

Federal investigators said the fire was accidental and was probably caused by an electrical malfunction or overheating in the warehouse’s cooling system. The flames ignited stored combustible material before spreading into the day-care facility through the roof and ceiling area.

The fire advanced rapidly because of highly flammable construction and insulation materials, investigators found. Smoke and toxic gases filled the center before many of the children could be moved to safety.

Subsequent federal and judicial reviews identified a series of safety failures, including inadequate emergency exits, shortcomings in fire detection and suppression, and weaknesses in government inspection and oversight. Accounts of the investigation also cited problems involving the building’s internal layout and the speed with which heat and smoke traveled through the ceiling.

Mexico’s Supreme Court later concluded that serious violations of constitutional rights had occurred and that numerous federal, state and municipal officials had failed in their responsibilities. The court’s inquiry was not itself a criminal judgment, but it reinforced families’ claims that the scale of the disaster reflected more than a single electrical fault.

## Witnesses describe chaotic rescue

Witnesses said smoke quickly became so dense that visibility inside the day care fell to almost nothing. Staff members carried children out through available doors while people outside tried to create additional openings.

Neighbors, motorists and workers rushed toward the burning building after hearing cries and seeing smoke. Rescuers smashed windows and punched holes through exterior walls. In one of the most widely reported rescue efforts, men used vehicles to tear through sections of wall so children could be pulled from the smoke-filled rooms.

Survivors and witnesses described children being passed from person to person outside the center, some unconscious and covered in soot. Adults attempted CPR on the pavement while ambulances carried the most seriously injured to local hospitals.

Parents arriving at the scene encountered confusion as authorities moved children to multiple medical facilities. Many searched from hospital to hospital for hours, trying to learn whether their sons or daughters had survived.

## Death toll rose after the fire

Early official reports listed fewer fatalities, but the toll increased as critically injured children died from burns and smoke inhalation.

The final widely recognized figure was:

- **49 children killed**
- **More than 100 children and adults injured**

The victims were generally described as ranging from infancy to about 5 years old.

Because casualty counts changed during the first days and some agencies counted smoke-inhalation cases differently, contemporary reports varied on the exact number injured or hospitalized. Dozens of children required treatment, and many suffered extensive burns, lung damage or both.

## Children transferred for specialized treatment

Hospitals in Hermosillo were quickly overwhelmed. Children in the most serious condition were placed on ventilators and treated in intensive-care and burn units.

Some patients were transferred to specialized hospitals elsewhere in Mexico, including facilities in Guadalajara and Mexico City. Others were flown to burn centers in the United States, including the Shriners pediatric facility in Sacramento, California.

Medical officials said smoke inhalation was a major concern even among children who did not appear to have the worst external burns. Several remained in critical condition for days or weeks, and later deaths among those patients pushed the fatality count higher.

Survivors faced repeated surgeries, skin grafts, respiratory treatment and long-term rehabilitation. Some were left with permanent scarring or chronic lung and mobility problems.

## Questions over inspections and political connections

ABC Day Care was privately operated under contract with Mexico’s federal social-security system, the **Mexican Social Security Institute**, known by its Spanish initials, IMSS.

Records and later inquiries showed that the center had been inspected and allowed to continue operating despite safety concerns. Investigators examined whether fire codes had been properly enforced and whether the facility had adequate evacuation routes, alarms and fire-resistant construction.

Public anger intensified after it emerged that some of the center’s owners had family or political connections to prominent figures in Sonora. Families alleged that those relationships helped shield the operators and officials from accountability. The owners denied knowingly placing children at risk.

A central issue was the division of responsibility among the private operators, IMSS, state authorities and municipal civil-protection agencies. Different offices had authority over licensing, inspections, building conditions and emergency preparedness, allowing officials to blame one another for the failures.

## Long fight for accountability

Parents formed advocacy groups and held annual marches demanding prosecutions, compensation and broader reforms. The phrase **“ABC nunca más” — “Never again ABC”** became a rallying cry.

Numerous public employees, inspectors and day-care personnel were investigated or charged over the years. Court decisions produced a complicated and often changing legal outcome, with some convictions, appeals and overturned rulings. Families repeatedly said the senior officials responsible for overseeing the system had not been adequately punished.

The disaster also led Mexico to strengthen child-care safety rules. A federal law adopted afterward established stricter standards for day-care centers, including requirements involving emergency exits, evacuation planning, inspections, staff training and the use of safer building materials.

For the families, however, regulatory changes did not end the case. Each June, relatives gather to name the 49 children and renew demands for full accountability — a reminder that what began as a warehouse fire became a national symbol of institutional negligence.
